'''Afghan''' (af′gan), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [A native name, derived by Afghan chroniclers from ''Afghāna'', a mythical grandson of Saul, king of Israel.] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A native or an inhabitant of Afghanistan, a mountainous country lying northwest of British India, south of Asiatic Russia, and east of Persia; distinctively, a member of the principal or dominant race of Afghanistan, speaking the Afghan language, the other inhabitants generally speaking Persian.—'''2.''' The language of the Afghans, called by themselves ''Pushtu'' or ''Pukhtu'', of Aryan affinity, though formerly supposed by some to be Semitic.—'''3.''' [''l. c.''] A kind of blanket made of knitted or crocheted wool, used as a sofa-cover or as a carriage-robe.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Pertaining or relating to Afghanistan or its people.

'''afield''' (ạ-fēld′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.'' [< ME. ''a felde'', ''o felde'', ''o feld'', < AS. ''on felda'' (dat.), ''on feld'' (acc.): ''on'', E. ''a''<sup>3</sup>, on, in; ''feld'', E. ''field''.] '''1.''' In or to the field or fields: as, “we drove ''afield'',”
readings.c2s1:
'''2.''' Figuratively, moving; passing from place to place; in circulation: as, a rumor is ''afloat.''
{{smaller block|I should like to know how much gossip there is ''afloat'' that the minister does not know.
{{right|''C. D. Warner'', Backlog Studies, p. 144.}}}}
'''3.''' Unfixed; moving without guide or control: as, our affairs are all ''afloat.''—'''4.''' In a state of overflow; flooded: as, the main deck was ''afloat.''—'''5.''' On board ship; at sea: as, cargo ''afloat'' and ashore.

'''aflow''' (ạ-flō′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''flow.''] In a loose, waving state; flowing: as, “with gray hair ''aflow,''” ''Whittier.''

'''afoam''' (ạ-fōm′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''foam.''] In a state of foam; foaming: as, the water was all ''afoam.''

'''afoot''' (ạ-fu̇t′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.'' [< ME. ''a fote, on fote,'' earlier with pl. ''a foten,'' < AS. ''on fōtum: on,'' E. ''a''<sup>3</sup>, on; ''fōtum,'' dat. pl. of ''fōt,'' E. ''foot.''] '''1.''' On foot; walking: opposed to on horseback, or in a carriage or other conveyance: as, he was mounted, but I came ''afoot.''—'''2.''' In a condition to walk about, as after sickness.
{{smaller block|He distinguished himself as a sick-nurse, till his poor comrade got ''afoot'' again. {{right|''Carlyle.''}}}}
'''3.''' Astir; stirring; about.
{{smaller block|<poem>When thy eager hand,
With game ''afoot,'' unslipped the hungry pack.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', Southern Statesman.}}}}

'''Afrancesado''' (Sp. pron. ä-frän-thā-sä′dō), ''n.'' [Sp., lit. Frenchified, pp. of ''afrancesar'', Frenchify, < ''á'' (L. ''ad''), to, + ''Francés'', < ML. ''Francensis'', French: see ''French''.] A member of that party in Spain which during the war of independence (1808–14) supported the French government of the country.

'''afreet''' (a-frēt′), ''n.'' Same as ''afrit''.

'''afresca†''', ''adv.'' [Prop. ''afresco'', < It. ''affresco'', ''a fresco'': ''a'', < L. ''ad'', to; ''fresco'', fresh, fresco: see ''fresco''.] In fresco. ''Evelyn''.

'''afresh''' (ạ-fresh′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' [< ''a''<sup>4</sup> (for ''of'', as in ''anew'') + ''fresh''.] Anew; again; after intermission.
{{smaller block|They crucify to themselves the Son of God ''afresh''.
{{right|Heb. vi. 6.}}
Not a few of the sites of the Roman cities were in after times occupied ''afresh'' as English towns.
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Amer. Lects., p. 130.}}}}

'''Afric''' (af′ric), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< L. ''Africus'': see following.] Same as ''African'': as, “''Afric'' shore,” ''Milton'', P. L., i. 585.
{{smaller block|Then will the ''Afric'' indeed have changed his skin and the leopard his spots.
{{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXXIII. 446.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>Wedded be thou to the hags of hell,
For daring to ''affy'' a mighty lord
Unto the daughter of a worthless king.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iv. 1.}}}}
'''5.''' To engage; bind; join.
{{smaller block|Personal respects rather seem to ''affy'' me unto that synod.
{{right|''Bp. Mountagu'', Appeal to Cæsar, p. 69.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To trust; confide.
{{smaller block|<poem>I do ''affy''
In thy uprightness and integrity.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., i. 1.}}}}

'''Afghan''' (af′gan), ''n.'' and ''a.''  [A native name, derived by Afghan chroniclers from ''Afghāna'', a mythical grandson of Saul, king of Israel.]  '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A native or an inhabitant of Afghanistan, a mountainous country lying northwest of British India, south of Asiatic Russia, and east of Persia; distinctively, a member of the principal or dominant race of Afghanistan, speaking the Afghan language, the other inhabitants generally speaking Persian.—'''2.''' The language of the Afghans, called by themselves ''Pushtu'' or ''Pukhtu'', of Aryan affinity, though formerly supposed by some to be Semitic.—'''3.''' [''l. c.''] A kind of blanket made of knitted or crocheted wool, used as a sofa-cover or as a carriage-robe.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Pertaining or relating to Afghanistan or its people.

'''afield''' (ạ-fēld′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.''  [< ME. ''a felde'', ''o felde'', ''o feld'', < AS. ''on felda'' (dat.), ''on feld'' (acc.): ''on'', E. ''a''<sup>3</sup>, on, in; ''feld'', E. ''field''.]  '''1.''' In or to the field or fields: as, “we drove ''afield'',” Milton'', Lycidas, l. 27; “Æneas is ''afield,''” ''Shak.'', T. and C., v. 3.
{{smaller block|What keeps Gurth so long ''afield?'' {{right|''Scott'', Ivanhoe.}}}}
'''2.''' Abroad; off the beaten path; far and wide.
{{smaller block|Why should he wander ''afield'' at the age of fifty-five?
{{right|''Trollope.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Without travelling further ''afield'' for illustrations, it will suffice if we note these relations of causes and effects in early European times.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Sociol., § 375.}}}}

'''afile†''', ''v. t.'' See ''affile.''

'''afire''' (ạ-fīr′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.''  [< ME. ''afire, afyre, afyr, afere, afure, o fure'' (also ''in fire''): ''a, o'', E. ''a''<sup>3</sup>; ''fyre'', E. ''fire.'']  On fire.
{{smaller block|The match is left ''afire.'' ''Fletcher'', Island Princess, ii. 1.
<poem>His heart ''afire''
With foolish hope.</poem>
{{right|''W. Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 131.}}}}

'''aflame''' (ạ-flām′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.''  [< ''a''<sup>3</sup>, on, + ''flame.'']  On fire; in or into flame; ablaze.
{{smaller block|The explosions, once begun, were continued at intervals till the mine was all ''aflame'' and had to be flooded.
{{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XX. 425.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Aflame'' with a glory beyond that of amber and amethyst. {{right|''George Eliot.''}}}}

'''aflat''' (ạ-flat′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.''  [< ''a''<sup>3</sup>, on, + ''flat''<sup>1</sup>.]  On a level with the ground; flatly.
{{smaller block|Lay all his branches ''aflat'' upon the ground.
{{right|''Bacon'', Nat. Hist., § 426.}}}}

'''aflaunt''' (ạ-flänt′ or ạ-flânt′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.''  [< ''a''<sup>3</sup>, on, + ''flaunt.'']  Flaunting or flauntingly; with showy equipage or dress.
{{smaller block|His hat all ''aflaunt'' and befeathered with all kinds of coloured plumes.
{{right|''Copley'', Wits, Fits, and Fancies (1614), p. 29.}}}}

'''aflight†''', ''v. t.''  [< ME. ''aflight'', pret., after ''aflight'', p. a.: see ''aflight'', ''p. a.'', and ''afflict'', ''v.'' The ME. spelling with ''gh'' may be due to the influence of ME. ''afright'', affrighted, and words of similar spelling; but cf. ''delight''.]  To terrify; alarm.
{{smaller block|<poem>Cam never yet . . . to mannes sight
Merveille which so sore ''aflight''
A mannes herte as it tho dede [then did].</poem>
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., i. 327.}}}}

'''aflight†''', ''p. a.''  [ME., < OF. ''aflit'', later ''afflict'', < L. ''afflictus'', pp.: see ''afflict'', ''p. a.'']  Afflicted; distressed.
{{smaller block|<poem>Her herte was so sore ''aflight''
That she ne wiste what to thinke.</poem>
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., ii. 309.}}}}

'''aflighted†''', ''p. a.''  [< ''aflight'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]  Same as ''aflight''.
{{smaller block|Judas . . . tooke a speciall pleasure to see them so ''aflighted''. {{right|''Sir T. More'', Works, p. 1389.}}}}

'''afloat''' (a-flōt′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.''  [< ME. ''aflote'', ''on flote'', < AS. ''on flote'' (dat.), ''on flot'' (acc.): ''on'', E. ''a''<sup>3</sup>, on, in; ''flot'', water deep enough to allow a ship or boat to float (cf. ''flota'', a ship); = Icel. ''ā floti'' (dat.), ''ā flot'' (acc.), afloat. The OF. ''a flot'', afloat, is of wholly different origin. See ''float''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'' and ''v.'']  '''1.''' Borne on the water; in a floating condition: as, the ship is ''afloat''.
{{smaller block|It was not without constant exertion that we kept ''afloat'', baling out the scud that broke over us, and warding off the ice with boat-hooks. {{right|''Kane'', Sec. Grinn. Exp., II. 264.}}}}
{{smaller block|Seventy per cent. of all the shipping ''afloat'' now use the Greenwich meridian. {{right|''Science'', IV. 377.}}}} '''2.''' Figuratively, moving; passing from place to place; in circulation: as, a rumor is ''afloat.''
{{smaller block|I should like to know how much gossip there is ''afloat'' that the minister does not know.
{{right|''C. D. Warner'', Backlog Studies, p. 144.}}}}
'''3.''' Unfixed; moving without guide or control: as, our affairs are all ''afloat.''—'''4.''' In a state of overflow; flooded: as, the main deck was ''afloat.''—'''5.''' On board ship; at sea: as, cargo ''afloat'' and ashore.

'''aflow''' (ạ-flō′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.''  [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''flow.'']  In a loose, waving state; flowing: as, “with gray hair ''aflow,''” ''Whittier.''

'''afoam''' (ạ-fōm′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.''  [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''foam.'']  In a state of foam; foaming: as, the water was all ''afoam.''

'''afoot''' (ạ-fu̇t′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.''  [< ME. ''a fote, on fote,'' earlier with pl. ''a foten,'' < AS. ''on fōtum: on,'' E. ''a''<sup>3</sup>, on; ''fōtum,'' dat. pl. of ''fōt,'' E. ''foot.'']  '''1.''' On foot; walking: opposed to on horseback, or in a carriage or other conveyance: as, he was mounted, but I came ''afoot.''—'''2.''' In a condition to walk about, as after sickness.
{{smaller block|He distinguished himself as a sick-nurse, till his poor comrade got ''afoot'' again. {{right|''Carlyle.''}}}}
'''3.''' Astir; stirring; about.
{{smaller block|<poem>When thy eager hand,
With game ''afoot,'' unslipped the hungry pack.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', Southern Statesman.}}}} 4. In progress; in course of being carried out: as, there is mischief ''afoot.''

'''afore''' (a̤-fōr′), ''adv.'', ''prep.'', and ''conj.''  [< ME. ''afore'', ''aforn'', ''aforne'', ''aforen'', < AS. ''on-foran'', before, < ''on'', on, + ''foran'', at the front. With ME. ''afore'' was merged early ME. ''atfore'', < AS. ''æt-foran'', < ''æt'', at, + ''foran'': see ''a-''<sup>2</sup>, ''a-''<sup>7</sup>, and ''fore'', and cf. ''before''. ''Afore'' is nearly obsolete in literary use, though still common in colloq. and dial. speech; cf. ''ahint''.]  '''I.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' Before in place; in front: especially in nautical phraseology.
{{smaller block|Will you go on ''afore?'' {{right|''Shak.'', Othello, v. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' Before in time; previously.
{{smaller block|If he have never drunk wine ''afore'', it will go near to remove his fit. {{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, ii. 2.}}}}

'''II.''' ''prep.'' '''1.''' Before in time.
{{smaller block|If your diligence be not speedy, I shall be there ''afore'' you. {{right|''Shak.'', Lear, i. 5.}}}}
'''2.''' Before in place; ''naut.'', further forward or nearer the bows than: as, ''afore'' the windlass.—'''3.''' Before in position, station, or rank.
{{smaller block|In this Trinity none is ''afore'' or after other. {{right|''Athanasian Creed.''}}}}
'''4.''' In or into the presence of; under the regard or notice of.
{{smaller block|''Afore'' God, I speak simply. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man out of his Humour, ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Notwithstanding all the dangers I laid ''afore'' you. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Epicœne, iii. 5.}}}}

'''Afore the mast.''' {{smaller|See ''before''.}}

'''III.''' ''conj.'' Before that; before; rather than.
<poem>''Afore'' I’ll
Endure the tyranny of such a tongue
And such a pride.</poem>{{right|''B. Jonson'', Magnetick Lady.}}

'''aforegoing''' (a̤-fōr′gō″ing), ''a.''  [< ''afore'' + ''going.'']  Going before; foregoing.

'''aforehand''' (a̤-fōr′hand), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' and ''a.''  [ME. ''aforehande'', also ''afor the hond''; < ''afore'' + ''hand.'' Cf. ''beforehand.'']  '''I.''' ''adv.'' Beforehand; in advance; in anticipation.
{{smaller block|She is come ''aforehand'' to anoint my body. {{right|Mark xiv. 8.}}}}
'''II.''' ''a.'' Beforehand in condition; forehanded: as, he is ''aforehand'' with the world.
{{smaller block|''Aforehand'' in all matters of power.
{{right|''Bacon'', War with Spain.}}}}

'''aforementioned''' (a̤-fōr′men″shọnd), ''a.'' Mentioned before; forementioned.

'''aforenamed''' (a̤-fōr′nāmd), ''a.'' Named before.

'''aforesaid''' (a̤-fōr′sed), ''a.''  [ME. ''aforseyd''; < ''afore'' + ''said.'']  Said, recited, or mentioned before, or in a preceding part of the same writing or discourse: common in legal use.

'''aforethought''' (a̤-fōr′thât), ''a.'' and ''n.''  [< ''afore'' + ''thought, pp.'']  '''I.''' ''a.'' Thought of beforehand; premeditated; prepense: used in law.—'''Malice aforethought.''' {{smaller|See ''malice''.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' [< ''afore'' + ''thought, n.''] Premeditation; forethought. [Rare.]

'''aforetime''' (a̤-fōr′tīm), ''adv.''  [< ''afore, adv.,'' + ''time.'']  In time past; in a former time.
{{smaller block|For whatsoever things were written ''aforetime'' were written for our learning. {{right|Rom. xv. 4.}}}}

'''aforn†''', ''adv.'' and ''prep.'' Obsolete form of ''afore.''

'''afornens†''', ''prep.'' and ''adv.''  [ME., also ''aforyens'', ''avoreye'', ''aforn ȝens'', < ''afore'', ''aforn'', before, + ''ȝens'', etc., against: see ''afore'', ''aforn'', and ''against'', and cf. ''fornenst.'']  '''I.''' ''prep.'' Over against; opposite.
{{smaller block|The yonder hous that stent ''aforyens'' us.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, ii. 1188.}}}}
'''II.''' ''adv.'' Over against.
{{smaller block|The centurien that stood ''aforn aȝens.''
{{right|''Wyclif'', Mark xv. 39. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}

'''a fortiori''' (ā fôr-shi-ō′rī).  [L.; lit., from a stronger (sc. cause): ''a'' for ''ab'', from; ''fortiori'', abl. of ''fortior'', ''fortius'', compar. of ''fortis'', strong: see ''fort.'']  For a still stronger reason; all the more. {{smaller|A phrase used in, and sometimes employed as the designation of, a kind of argument, which concludes either (''a'') that something does not take place, because the causes which alone could bring it to pass operate still more strongly in another case without producing that effect; or (''b'') that something does take place, because causes much weaker than those which operate to bring it about are effective in another case. An argument of the latter kind is the following: “If God so clothe the grass of the field, which to-day is and to-morrow is cast into the oven, shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?” Mat. vi. 30.}}
{{smaller block|As he [Shakspere] has avoided obscurities in his sonnets, he would do so ''a fortiori'' in his plays, both for the purpose of immediate effect on the stage and of future appreciation. {{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 1st ser., p. 165.}}}}

'''afoul''' (a̤-foul′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.''  [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''foul.'']  In a state of collision or entanglement: with ''of'': as, a ship with its shrouds afoul;'' the brig ran ''afoul of'' the steamer.—'''To fall afoul of''', {{smaller|to assail violently; attack vigorously in any way: as, he ''fell afoul of'' him tooth and nail, or with an envenomed pen.}}

'''afraid''' (a̤-frād′), ''a.''  [< ME. ''afraied'', etc., pp. of ''afraien'', etc., > E. ''affray'', frighten: see ''affray'', ''v.'' Not connected with ''afeard''.]  Impressed with fear or apprehension; fearful: followed by ''of'' before the object of fear, where that is not an infinitive: as, to be ''afraid of'' death; I am ''afraid'' to go.
{{smaller block|Be of good cheer: it is I; be not ''afraid''. {{right|Mat. xiv. 27.}}}}
{{smaller block|Whistling, to keep myself from being ''afraid''.
{{right|''Dryden'', Amphitryon, iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A man who’s not ''afraid'' to say his say,
Though a whole town’s against him.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', John Endicott, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|='''Syn.''' ''Afraid, Frightened, Terrified,'' timid, shy, apprehensive, troubled, suspicious, distrustful. ''Afraid'' expresses a less degree of fear than ''frightened'' or ''terrified'', which describe outward states. In colloquial language, I am ''afraid'' is often nearly equivalent to I suspect, I am inclined to think, or the like, and is regularly used as a kind of polite introduction to a correction, objection, etc., or to make a statement sound less positive: as, I am ''afraid'' you are wrong; I am ''afraid'' that argument won’t hold.
<poem>And there is ev’n a happiness
That makes the heart ''afraid''.</poem>
{{right|''Hood'', Melancholy.}}}}
{{smaller block|Antony, on the other hand, was desirous to have him there, fancying that he would . . . be ''frightened'' into a compliance. {{right|''C. Middleton'', Life of Cicero, III. ix.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Airy ghosts,
That work no mischief, ''terrify'' us more
Than men in steel with bloody purposes.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|{{right|''T. B. Aldrich'', Set of Turquoise.}}}}

'''Afrancesado''' (Sp. pron. ä-frän-thā-sä′dō), ''n.''  [Sp., lit. Frenchified, pp. of ''afrancesar'', Frenchify, < ''á'' (L. ''ad''), to, + ''Francés'', < ML. ''Francensis'', French: see ''French''.]  A member of that party in Spain which during the war of independence (1808–14) supported the French government of the country.

'''afreet''' (a-frēt′), ''n.'' Same as ''afrit''.

'''afresca†''', ''adv.''  [Prop. ''afresco'', < It. ''affresco'', ''a fresco'': ''a'', < L. ''ad'', to; ''fresco'', fresh, fresco: see ''fresco''.]  In fresco.  ''Evelyn''.

'''afresh''' (ạ-fresh′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.''  [< ''a''<sup>4</sup> (for ''of'', as in ''anew'') + ''fresh''.]  Anew; again; after intermission.
{{smaller block|They crucify to themselves the Son of God ''afresh''.
{{right|Heb. vi. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|Not a few of the sites of the Roman cities were in after times occupied ''afresh'' as English towns.
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Amer. Lects., p. 130.}}}}

'''Afric''' (af′ric), ''a.'' and ''n.''  [< L. ''Africus'': see following.]  Same as ''African'': as, “''Afric'' shore,” ''Milton'', P. L., i. 585.
{{smaller block|Then will the ''Afric'' indeed have changed his skin and the leopard his spots.
{{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXXIII. 446.}}}}

'''African''' (af′ri-kan), ''a.'' and ''n.''  [< L. ''Africanus'', < ''Africa'', name of the country, prop. fem. of ''Africus'', a., < ''Afer'', an African, a word of Phenician (Carthaginian) origin.]  '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Pertaining to Africa: either (''a'') to the continent of that name, or (''b'') to the region about Carthage, the ancient Roman province of Africa.—'''2.''' Of or belonging to the black race of Africa; characteristic of or peculiar to negroes: as, ''African'' features; ''African'' cheerfulness.—'''African almond, cubebs, goose,''' etc. {{smaller|See the nouns.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A native of the continent, or in ancient times of the province, of Africa.—'''2.''' A member of the black African race; a negro.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
